scenario: Today's inference-systems thread replaces fixed settings in inference serving with ones measured and adjusted to load. TableTune turns the table of how many tokens speculative decoding guesses per step into something measured and self-correcting in production. FlatCake stores the KV cache with memory and SSD at the same level. ConfluxServe lets prefill and decode share a batch while each keeps its own parallelism. Rimuru lets expert weights and the KV cache share one pool of GPU memory. On the training side, TIDE removes the back-and-forth copies in FSDP2 communication, and an SGLang security write-up explains how, under disaggregated serving, KV cache data leaked into other users' requests.

papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Abhishek Malvankar, Paul Castro, Nick Mitchell, Lionel Villard
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.
papers.summary: The table in vLLM's documentation that sets how many tokens speculative decoding guesses per step at each batch size can visibly cut throughput on a different GPU or model. This paper gives a tool that measures the best table in minutes and keeps correcting it as traffic changes. Speculation only pays while the GPU has spare compute, so the more requests share a batch, the fewer tokens each step should guess. TableTune times every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and picks the highest-throughput table. Once in production, a plugin reads vLLM's counts of accepted guesses, combines them with the measured step times, and rewrites the table with the length that yields the most useful tokens per second at each batch size. On a mixture-of-experts model, against the fastest fixed draft length at each load, the documented table is up to 18% slower and the measured table at most 3% slower.

papers.title: FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xin Huang, Teng Ma, Zhuoran Li, Yibo Zhao, Zhaoshi Li, Qianchao Zhu, Wei Yang, Chenxi Wang, Tao Xie, Youwei Zhuo
papers.abstract: KV cache reuse accelerates LLM serving, but existing systems manage host DRAM and NVMe SSD as a tiered hierarchy where DRAM acts as an intermediate cache. Production LLM workloads break both premises of this hierarchy. First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering, since workloads are dominated either by one-shot blocks with long reuse distances or by multi-gigabyte agentic sessions that exceed DRAM capacity, putting SSD on the critical read path. Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration. Holding host staging buffers for in-flight prefixes causes contention under load that aborts prefetches, while incremental eviction scatters a session's blocks across the SSD and prevents large sequential reads. We present FlatCake, a flat KV storage architecture that exposes host DRAM and NVMe SSD as peer media in a unified 64-bit address space. Exploiting the fact that KV blocks are write-once, immutable, and reused at session scope, FlatCake places each block directly onto its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order at creation time and never migrates it. FlatCake streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage and decouples DRAM and SSD request queues to prevent head-of-line blocking. On a production Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, FlatCake sustains a 94% cache hit rate as load increases (versus 64% for Mooncake), eliminates Mooncake's $6.5\times$--$6.7\times$ SSD read amplification, and reduces peak-load mean TTFT by $1.6\times$ while improving total token throughput by $1.6\times$. Across 8K--128K contexts on Llama-3.1-70B, FlatCake further reduces mean TTFT by up to $2.4\times$ over Mooncake and $1.8\times$ over Mooncake-GDS.
papers.summary: After analyzing eight production LLM request traces, the authors find that the common practice of treating host memory as a KV cache layer in front of the SSD barely filters any reads under these workloads. Reused blocks either come back only after a long gap, or belong to agent sessions of several gigabytes each that memory cannot hold, so the SSD always ends up on the read path. FlatCake puts memory and SSD at the same level and decides each block's home when it is created. Shared system prompts and short-reply chats go to memory, while multi-gigabyte agent sessions are written straight to the SSD. A session's blocks are stored contiguously and never move, and reads stream large chunks from the SSD straight into the GPU. Replaying a production Claude Code trace, the share of prefixes it reads back instead of recomputing holds at 94% as load rises, while Mooncake drops to 64%. KV storage for long agent sessions should be planned per session.

papers.title: ConfluxServe: Reconciling Resource Utilization and Parallelism Efficiency across Prefill and Decode in LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Prefill and decode are complementary in resource usage, but often divergent in parallelism preferences. Executing the two phases separately preserves their preferred parallelism but leaves complementary resources underutilized, while co-batching improves utilization but often requires a uniform parallel configuration that hurts execution efficiency. To resolve this utilization-efficiency dilemma, we propose Conflux Parallelism (XP), a parallel execution abstraction that co-executes prefill and decode with different parallelism within the same batch. Conflux Parallelism exploits operator-level Transformer structure to construct a heterogeneous execution path with different batching and parallelism strategies across operators, combining the best of co-batching and phase-specific execution. Building on Conflux Parallelism, we design ConfluxServe, an SLO-aware serving system that maximizes cluster goodput under TTFT and TBT constraints. Evaluation on production workloads shows that ConfluxServe improves serving goodput by 1.26-1.62x over the strongest baselines.
papers.summary: In LLM serving, running prefill and decode together lets their resource needs complement each other, since prefill uses compute and decode uses memory bandwidth. But the two want different parallelism. A long-prompt prefill must spread across more GPUs to deliver the first token on time, while decode needs only a few. ConfluxServe treats each operator differently. In the linear layers, tokens from both phases form one batch and are computed together under the same weight sharding. At the attention layers they split: decode stays on its own group of GPUs, while prefill spreads across more GPUs through two All-to-All exchanges. Both paths run at the same time and merge back into one batch afterwards. On production workloads, the request rate it sustains within latency targets is 1.26 to 1.62 times that of the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.
papers.summary: Open models built for agents often have to choose between capability and inference cost. NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super optimizes both. It is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model that activates only about a tenth of its parameters per token, and it scores 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, ahead of the previous-generation Ultra with several times more active parameters. The deployment design matters more to people who serve models. The model carries its own multi-token prediction head for speculative decoding, and post-training trains that head again, raising the average number of accepted tokens per step by up to 21.8% over the untrained head. With NVFP4 quantization, throughput on an interactive agent workload is 2.43 times that of BF16. Base, post-trained and quantized weights are released together with the training data.

papers.title: The Endgame of FSDP Communication: Layout-Aware Collectives on Copy Engines, RDMA, and NVSwitch
papers.authors: Zejian Wang, Yifan Zhao, Kaihui Ren, Xiaoling Zhou, Yubin Wang, Chenhao Guan, Lin Zhang, Yufeng Li, Zhikang Mo, Zhuoru Ma, Yingtong Xiong, Jihu Guo, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song
papers.abstract: Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2) maintains parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors, whereas its collective path operates on flat, rank-major buffers. Converting between these layouts copies all-gather outputs into parameter storage and packs gradients into full-group fp32 buffers. Layout conversion alone accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training at 8K tokens per GPU. Communication kernels impose a second cost: a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM that would otherwise complete in a single wave by 69%. We present TIDE, a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs. TIDE preserves FSDP2's per-parameter storage and compute kernels while folding layout placement into collective addressing. TIDE-AG delivers shards directly to parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, with no SMs used for transport or placement. TIDE-RS consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients directly and reduces them into fp32 shards (a mixed-precision mode that NCCL does not provide) using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks (CTAs) for node-local accumulation and NVSwitch for cross-node reduction. A two-phase pipeline separates gradient reads from network progress; Slot-Reuse optionally stages gradients in vacated all-gather slots. On 64 GPUs, TIDE reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% relative to FSDP2+SymmMem across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2, and Qwen3-30B-A3B. It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by factors of 12.5-14.5 and cuts interference with concurrent compute by up to an order of magnitude. Its reduce-scatter buffer remains nearly constant from 16 to 64 GPUs at a fixed per-GPU output size, and its peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2+SymmMem's and, with Slot-Reuse on Wan2.2, below Stock FSDP2's.
papers.summary: The Kling team's TIDE builds the layout conversion that FSDP2 performs every step directly into communication. Stock FSDP2 stores parameters and gradients one tensor per parameter, but NCCL only sends and receives one flat buffer ordered by GPU, so every step copies data back and forth. TIDE has communication read from where each parameter lives and write straight to where it must end up, with copy engines, RDMA and NVSwitch moving the data and no change to model code or compute kernels. Across three models, step time drops by up to 27.1% relative to stock FSDP2. ==Beyond raw communication speed, data layout and contention for compute decide training speed as well==.

deep_reading.title: The Endgame of FSDP Communication: Layout-Aware Collectives on Copy Engines, RDMA, and NVSwitch

papers.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
papers.authors: Zhiyuan Fang, Dingyang Li, Jianfeng Zhong, Bin Wang, Weixi Zhu, Cunshu Ni, Zicong Hong, Wuhui Chen, Zibin Zheng
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
papers.summary: To run a large MoE model on a machine with limited GPU memory, the usual approach keeps some expert weights in host memory and moves them onto the GPU when needed. Even so, GPU memory is still split into two fixed regions, one for experts and one for the KV cache. Under heavy load the KV cache runs short and concurrency stalls. Under light load the KV cache region sits idle but cannot hold extra experts, so expert weights keep being moved back and forth. Rimuru puts both into one shared page pool and adjusts it with load. When requests pile up, more experts leave GPU memory to make room for the KV cache, and when traffic drops, experts move back. To make this work, each kind of data manages the same pool with its own page size, and a rewritten MoE kernel reads expert weights that are not stored contiguously. On two consumer GPUs under heavy load, throughput reaches up to 19.03 times that of KTransformers.

deep_reading.title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading

papers.title: SGLang security update: improving request isolation
papers.abstract: On September 9, 2026, Cloudflare notified us of cross-request KV cache exposure in its GLM-5.3 deployment on Workers AI. We worked with Cloudflare to address the request-rejection path involved and strengthen related cache-lifetime handling in disaggregated serving.
papers.summary: In one of Cloudflare's production model deployments, a request received content from another user's session. The SGLang team traced it to the path where prefill and decode run on separate workers. A request that exceeded the prefill KV cache capacity should have been rejected, yet it still went through the handoff, and decode read cache pages that had never been filled for it. They also fixed a related hazard. When a request is interrupted midway, RDMA writes already sent are still in flight, but decode had already returned the destination slots to the allocator, so the late data could land in another request's KV cache without any error. The fix releases the slots only after those writes are confirmed to have landed. On two H100 GPUs, throughput before and after the fix differs by less than 2%. Teams running disaggregated serving should upgrade and check that context length matches cache pool capacity.

papers.title: DualQuant: Dual-scale Calibration-free Weight-and-Activation Quantization for LLMs
papers.authors: Mahsa Salmani, Sayeh Sharify, Hesham Mostafa
papers.abstract: Low-bit inference on accelerators with native 4-bit support requires quantizing both weights and activations to realize the full throughput gains these formats provide. While post-training weight quantization has been extensively studied, activation quantization remains considerably more challenging and typically requires calibration data. In this work, we introduce DUALQUANT, a dual-scale, calibration-free post-training quantization framework that directly minimizes the weight-reconstruction Mean Squared Error (MSE) and, as an immediate by-product, yields per-channel activation rescalings prior to activation quantization. Our key observation is that the scaling factors obtained by minimizing weight-reconstruction error provide effective activation rescalings, enabling competitive activation quantization without calibration data. We formulate DUALQUANT as a non-differentiable weight-reconstruction problem and develop an efficient solver based on variable splitting and block coordinate descent, where each subproblem admits a closed-form update. DUALQUANT provides a unified algorithm supporting a wide range of formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4. To our knowledge, DUALQUANT is the first dual-scaling method to formally support MX and NV block formats. Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on WikiText-2, C4, and zero-shot downstream tasks, DUALQUANT matches or exceeds the accuracy of calibration-based SmoothQuant across most models and formats, and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, with large gains for MX and NV block formats. We validate these gains with a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The resulting implementation closely matches the accuracy of fake quantization while delivering up to 2.61x memory reduction and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over BF16.
papers.summary: To get the full speedup of new GPUs with native low-bit math, both weights and activations must be quantized to 4 bits. A few activation channels carry very large values, and the usual fix collects calibration data first and then scales those channels down. DualQuant shows this works without calibration data. It looks only at the weights. To make the quantized weights reconstruct the original weights as closely as possible, it solves for a scaling factor per input channel and multiplies that weight column by it. The same activation channel is then divided by the same factor, which leaves the matrix product unchanged, so these factors end up scaling the activations as well. It supports many formats, including INT4, MX and NVFP4, and on most models and formats it matches or beats the accuracy of SmoothQuant, which needs calibration data. Running real packed 4-bit inference on an RTX 4090, throughput reaches up to 2.46 times that of BF16.

papers.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
papers.authors: Mads Toftrup, Marco Federici, Boris van Breugel, Paul Whatmough, Markus Nagel
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.
papers.summary: Post-training quantization has to settle three things: each layer's value range, what transform to apply to weights and activations before quantizing, and which way to round each weight. Most methods handle one of these at a time, each minimizing the error at that layer's output, but a small error at one layer does not mean the model's final output changes little. The authors find that a layer's error barely predicts the final impact. It does once the error is weighted by sensitivity, an estimate of how much the model's final output changes when that layer's output shifts slightly in each direction. They then use an approximate Hessian to optimize all three under one objective: how much quantization changes the model's final output. With weights, activations and the KV cache all at 4 bits, it gets the lowest perplexity on all four models, and on the smallest model it lowers perplexity from the best baseline's 17.23 to 16.05.

papers.title: DWISE: Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine
papers.authors: Lie Li, Wen Li, Junxiao Shen, Jindong Gu, Guosheng Hu
papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs), diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising many tokens in parallel, offering a promising path to efficient inference. Existing serving frameworks, however, schedule dLLM requests with policies designed for AR models, namely first-come-first-served (FCFS) admission and prefill priority. We find that both policies are ill-suited to dLLMs, wasting much of their speed. FCFS ignores that a dLLM request's decoding cost is highly heterogeneous and unknown at arrival, causing severe head-of-line blocking. Prefill priority, widely used in AR-LLM serving to keep time-to-first-token low, sharply cuts dLLM efficiency, as rounds that run only prompts leave most of the batch idle. We present DWISE, a Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine for efficient dLLM serving. DWISE schedules requests by their remaining work, measured in a block-level unit shared by prefill and denoising, so both phases share a round. To predict the unknown denoising workload, DWISE combines a lightweight prompt-based predictor at admission with a single refinement from the first denoising round's hidden states, which capture model-specific information absent from the prompt and require no additional model execution. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on five models from three dLLM families under bursty workloads, DWISE reduces mean end-to-end latency over SGLang by 5.4$\times$ on average and up to 14.9$\times$ while preserving task accuracy. The code will be released publicly.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models denoise many tokens in parallel each round and promise much faster generation than producing one token at a time, but serving frameworks copy the scheduling of autoregressive models: first come, first served, and prefill first. The authors find both rules fit poorly. How many denoising rounds a request needs varies widely and is unknown at arrival, so first come, first served leaves short requests waiting behind long ones. Rounds that run only prompts leave most of the batch idle. These models generate in fixed-size blocks of tokens, and a prompt step and a denoising step each process one block at the same cost. DWISE therefore counts remaining work for both prefill and denoising in block rounds, runs requests with the least left first, and lets both phases share a round. Remaining rounds are first estimated by a small regression model from the prompt's word, line and token counts. After the first denoising round, the model's final-layer hidden states are averaged and passed to a two-layer network that re-estimates them once. Across five models on SGLang, stock SGLang's mean end-to-end latency is 5.4 times that of DWISE.
